webTitle: DHS officers raise concerns over potentially illegal voter searches and unreliable data, whistleblower says

fields.headline: DHS officers raise concerns over potentially illegal voter searches and unreliable data, whistleblower says
fields.trailText: Officers were instructed to search state voter databases and create federal records on suspected non-citizen voters despite concerns over the process
fields.bodyText: Department of Homeland Security (DHS) lawyers told officers investigating voter fraud they would not be held responsible for violating state laws around accessing voter registration information, an anonymous whistleblower revealed on Monday. DHS officers also had concerns about the reliability of the data they were working with, the whistleblower said. The Trump administration has ramped up its investigation into noncitizen voting ahead of the midterm elections. Noncitizen voting is extremely rare and the effort has only turned up a handful of cases so far. As part of the effort, officers tasked with investigating potential non-citizen voters were told to take data DHS had compiled on voters and run it through state websites where voters can look up their voter information. Some states require voters to click attestations affirming that they are looking up their own voter information. On the Virginia Department of Elections website, for example, voters must click a disclaimer that says: “I certify and affirm that the information provided to access my voter registration is my own or I am expressly authorized by the voter to access this information. I understand that it is unlawful to access the record of any other voter, punishable as computer fraud.” “In light of these instructions about access to the state websites, officers expressed concerns that accessing registered voter information on these websites may be illegal as officers are essentially misrepresenting themselves as the potential registered voter (with or without a specific attestation),” lawyers for Democracy Defenders Fund, who is representing the whistleblower, wrote in the disclosure. A slide in the presentation officers watched in the initiative says DHS’ office of the general counsel “advised that this type of review is permissible as open-source research when conducted for purposes related to adjudicative or investigative responsibilities”. It also said there was an effort to get further clarification from DHS leadership, and officers were told that immigration officers and immigration service officers “are not personally liable for conducting these searches when done as part of their official duties and properly documented”. “This statement suggests that there may be legal implications for accessing these websites, but that the officers themselves are simply not personally liable. This leads us to believe that USCIS-FDNS HQ is aware that the activity may be illegal, and yet they are still requiring officers to engage in this illegal activity with promises of personal liability protection,” lawyers for the whistleblower wrote. “Far from being rushed or untrained, these investigative efforts are conducted diligently and professionally. Identification and investigation of aliens who vote in our elections provides an essential guarantee in the authenticity of our election results. There is no quota on criminality. DHS will pursue each and every illegal voter to the fullest extent of the law,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. “One has to question why the media is so dead set on running a smoke screen for illegal alien voters in American elections.” The whistleblower also expressed concern about the reliability of the data DHS was giving officers to review as well as the lack of transparency into where the data came from. In some cases, DHS gave officers an individual’s name and specific dates on which they registered and voted. But when an officer went to look up the individual in the state’s voter registration website, there was no record of the voter. “With such a direct contradiction, knowing the specific source and date of the information is necessary to determine reliability before taking any action.” The whistleblower disclosure says this was a huge issue in California, where officers were often unable to access the voter registration database. Officers were told they should still create a file on the person in Tecs – a DHS database where law enforcement officials share information (Tecs is not an acronym). “The result is that a significant number of Tecs records, potentially thousands or tens of thousands, will be created against California residents based on data that an officer may have good reason to believe is unreliable or inaccurate without corroboration,” the disclosure says. “The whistleblower’s disclosure outlines shocking allegations of unlawful and unethical conduct that includes potentially thousands of violations of state law and the use of highly questionable data,” California senator Alex Padilla, a Democrat, said in a statement. Other election officials have raised concerns about the DHS data. Earlier this year, DHS told Nevada election officials it had identified as many as 15,903 non-citizens on its rolls. In a meeting last month, DHS representatives told the Nevada secretary of state’s office they had made that claim by comparing the state’s July 2025 public voter rolls against DHS data. When DHS began reviewing the data, they had only firmly identified 185 non-citizens on the rolls, though they said their review was ongoing. The disclosure also details the pressure the department put on officers to find voter fraud. Officers received their first and only training on 21 August, and were expected to begin researching four days later, lawyers for the whistleblower wrote. They were expected to review five individuals per hour. “The Department of Homeland Security is sending hundreds of officers who should be focused on our security on a wild goose chase to prove Trump’s long-debunked election conspiracy theories – and DHS is telling officers to lie to do it. This new DHS initiative is nothing more than an unlawful order by the government to silence the voices of Americans,” Senate minority leader Chuck Schumer said in a statement.

webTitle: First Thing: Oil prices surge as attacks on Saudi Arabia stoke supply fears

fields.headline: First Thing: Oil prices surge as attacks on Saudi Arabia stoke supply fears
fields.trailText: Strike on kingdom’s east-west pipeline could affect 4% of global oil supply
fields.bodyText: Good morning. Oil prices have climbed above $108 a barrel after a series of drone attacks from Iraq’s territory forced Saudi Arabia to close its east-west crude pipeline. Saudi traders said the kingdom would run out of oil stocks for export if it did not reopen within days. Gas prices also climbed higher. Energy prices have surged this year, as the US-Israel war with Iran has disrupted oil and gas supply across the Middle East. The spike came as the Iran-aligned Houthi forces in Yemen launched several attacks against Saudi Arabia and captured the strategic island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab strait on Sunday, expanding their control of the waterway. Where did the attack on Saudi Arabia come from? Iraq’s government confirmed the attacks were launched from its territory and ordered an investigation. Baghdad is under mounting pressure to stop militant groups – including those backed by Saudi Arabia’s regional rival Iran – launching attacks on Gulf countries from Iraqi soil. The US president, Donald Trump, said he believed Tehran was responsible. Why has Saudi Arabia been relying on its east-west pipeline? Riyadh has increased the use of the 745-mile pipeline since the start of the war on Iran in order to bypass the strait of Hormuz’s closure. The world’s biggest exporter has used the pipeline to reroute about 4m barrels a day – about 4% of global supply – but with the ‌pipeline out of service, the Red Sea port of Yanbu now has stocks to maintain exports for just five to seven days. AI-linked stocks take hit as leading US tech CEOs back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development AI-linked stocks have tumbled after the bosses of Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX called for a slowdown in “reckless” development, citing fears the technology could soon run out of control. The market swings come after the chief executive of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, appealed for the AI industry to “slow down”. Last week, a former Anthropic employee had warned that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The respective CEOs of OpenAI and SpaceX, Sam Altman and Elon Musk, have backed Amodei’s call. The US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”. What is the Anthropic CEO proposing? Robert Booth explains Amodei’s suggestion: first, each US AI company grants access to third-party evaluators; second, all companies in democratic countries establish common safety standards; and third, the world’s democratic AI powers coordinate with autocracies – notably China – to control the race. How has Barack Obama intervened over AI? The former US president made a direct appeal to Democrats to coalesce around a unified AI safety policy, arguing that waiting for voluntary compliance from tech firms was a recipe for governance failure. Israel accused of trying to ‘eliminate’ living conditions for Palestinians in West Bank Israel is working towards the systematic “elimination” of the conditions that sustain Palestinian collective life in the occupied West Bank, according to a report published by the human rights group B’Tselem. The Israeli organisation says Israel is “dramatically intensifying its attacks on every aspect of Palestinian life in the West Bank”. How does the report say Israel is making life intolerable? “Palestinian communities are being pushed out in an accelerating process of ethnic cleansing, while an ever-expanding Israeli presence is being established … Elimination in this context means sustained harm to the conditions that enable Palestinians to exist as a people with land, institutions, language, culture, social ties, leadership, shared memory and history, and a social and political horizon. It is an ongoing political project.” Wisconsin congressman swims to safety after plane makes emergency landing in lake A Republican congressman said he had to swim to safety after a plane he was traveling in made an emergency landing in a lake late Saturday. Tom Tiffany is running for governor on the Republican ticket in Wisconsin and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. Tiffany says he was returning from the La Crosse county Lincoln Day Dinner when the light aircraft lost power as it approached Wausau downtown airport. He said the pilot made an emergency landing in Lake Wausau and they ended up in the water and swam to safety. Emergency responders got Tiffany and the pilot to a nearby hospital, where they were treated for minor injuries. In other news … Sweden’s centre-left parties lead the country’s national election by just a single seat with most votes counted. The election authority said a preliminary vote count may not be ready until Thursday. Donald Trump has doubled down on his controversial pledge to give US adults a $5,000 “dividend” if the Republican ⁠party keeps control of Congress after the midterms. A San Jose police officer has been fired for using his department’s Flock license plate tracking system to share the location of a woman with the suspect accused of abusing her. A coroner in Pennsylvania has announced the death of a 40-year-old woman associated with the state’s ongoing measles outbreak. A newly unveiled statue of the rightwing activist Charlie Kirk was vandalized at the Turning Point USA headquarters. Sydney Sweeney has been accused of “sexualising women’s sport” by appearing naked in a sports betting prediction ad. Stat of the day: Who are the 514 people accused of starting French wildfires and what motivates them? Jon Henley reports from France where experts believe one-third of wildfires are set deliberately, with arson the biggest single cause of forest fires last year. Building Power: While Puerto Ricans protest for reliable access to water, the governor washes her hands Coral Murphy Marcos speaks to members of the Coalición Exigimos Agua (We Demand Water Coalition), residents of the San Juan neighborhood of Santurce, who are campaigning over the island’s water issues. Don’t miss this: The royal crown branded on enslaved Africans – Britain’s monarchy and the slave trade A major investigation reveals how generations of British monarchs were central to the slave trade. This interactive goes on to illustrate the register laying bare Britain’s slave-trading past, littered with the names of monarchs, MPs and merchants. … or this: From a giant arch to a nuke-proof bunker, Trump’s legacy-building blingfest is an architectural atrocity The United States’s modern “king” is reshaping Washington DC in his own image. The architecture and design critic Oliver Wainwright deplores the decorator-in-chief’s mutilation of the seat of the nation. Climate check: ‘Tidal wave’ of Pfas being launched to satisfy AI industry More bad news thanks to the growth of AI. Pfas companies are launching a “tidal wave” of forever-chemical production to meet demand from the industry, a campaign organisation has warned. Last Thing: Missing US hiker, 70, found injured on remote island after week-long search A 70-year-old hiker who had been missing for a week on a Michigan island was rescued at the weekend, according to the US Coast Guard. Even though Craig Berg was found injured and hypothermic on Isle Royale, he was “alive and alert”, according to a statement Sign up First Thing is delivered to thousands of inboxes every weekday. webTitle: Disaster insurance, datacenters, right to repair: meet the midterm candidates running on green policies

fields.headline: Disaster insurance, datacenters, right to repair: meet the midterm candidates running on green policies
fields.trailText: Some of the everyday struggles animating voters have a climate link lurking in the background
fields.bodyText: When Florida governor Ron DeSantis signed a law erasing the words “climate change” from state statutes in May 2024 – colloquially known as the “don’t say climate change” law – Democrats were outraged. Just six months later, many liberal politicians began to go quiet on the issue themselves. After Donald Trump won the 2024 election, mentions of the climate crisis started to disappear from Democrats’ rhetoric. As the 2026 midterms approach, that retreat is still shaping how some candidates talk about climate on the campaign trail. The trend, known as “climate-hushing”, may reflect the limitations of Joe Biden’s climate policies, said Daniel Aldana Cohen, assistant sociology professor at the University of California, Berkeley, who studies climate politics and inequality. Green jobs and housing investments fell short of the climate movement’s desires, consumer incentives disproportionately benefited wealthier households, and Democrats struggled to effectively communicate their accomplishments. The president has since rolled back many Biden-era clean energy incentives and regulations. The climate crisis, however, is still rearing its head around the country, fueling the heatwaves, wildfires and floods plaguing communities around the US. It also lurks behind issues animating voters, from datacenter expansion to rising home insurance rates. And while some pundits have concluded from their polling and research that Americans don’t want to hear about global warming, other surveys directly contradict those findings. “Maybe people don’t rank climate as their main or top issue … but nobody really experiences everyday life like walking around the world rank-ordering the things that they care about,” said Aldana Cohen, who is also founding co-director of the thinktank Climate and Community Institute that calls for “green economic populism”. “What’s important is to learn how to embed the climate issue organically amidst the other issues that people care most about.” Some progressive and populist candidates in the US midterms are pushing back against climate-hushing, linking the issue to economic concerns and everyday struggles. Others aren’t speaking about it directly, but pushing for policies that could curb emissions. Such efforts could help build a mass base for climate policies, said Aldana Cohen. “If we want to decarbonize fast enough and adapt to the impacts that are already here, we’re going to need a robust majority that backs those policies,” he said. “Elite consensus alone will not suffice … we’re going to need like large numbers of people really enthusiastic about climate policies.” The Guardian spoke with three midterm candidates about how three issues with major environmental implications are shaping their campaigns. Single-payer disaster insurance Jane Kim, state director of the Working Families Party and a former San Francisco county supervisor, is running to become California’s next insurance commissioner. The little-noticed but highly influential position oversees the state’s home, auto and business insurance markets. The frontrunner in the race, she received 27% of votes in the June primary. Among her key proposals is a single-payer system for disaster insurance, which she began developing as climate-fueled wildfires ravaged the state. California wildfires have catalyzed homeowners’ insurance crisis. Companies have stopped writing new policies and non-renewed thousands of homeowners in high-risk areas, making coverage increasingly difficult to find. Homeowners can turn to the California Fair Plan, the insurer of last resort, but it provides limited fire coverage rather than the broader protection of a typical homeowners policy. Kim argues that climate-fueled disasters are making catastrophic risk too large and socially consequential to leave to the private sector. “The biggest change in the insurance industry in the past four years is the increase of climate disasters,” she said. “We used to have a billion-dollar storm every three to four months, and it seems like we now have one every three weeks, so the price of risk has truly gone up.” The scheme would create a public, government-run insurance program to cover wildfire damage for all homes, modeled on government-backed programs in New Zealand, France and Spain. Homes would be automatically enrolled regardless of their condition, and owners would pay premiums based on property values, risk, and other factors. Some aspects of the plan would require legislative approval. Since the nonprofit program would not have to generate shareholder profits, Kim said investment returns could build a pool of money for future claims. It could also be designed to mitigate climate risk rather than simply avoid it, she added. “In New Zealand, they actually use a portion of premiums for fire-proofing and flood-proofing, because they guarantee home disaster insurance to everyone,” she said. Private insurers are also major institutional investors in oil and gas, which are fueling the climate crisis, said Kim – an issue she would uplift in office, though it is outside the direct purview of the role. Critics of the single-payer disaster scheme argue that shifting financial risk to the state could further destabilize California’s insurance market and leave taxpayers bearing a greater burden, and fear pricing risk either too high or too low could both cause major challenges. Kim argues consumers are already paying too much for insurance. She says revenues could be raised from a variety of places, including potentially by forcing state insurers to pay an “exit fee”. She also says she does not aim to eliminate the private insurance market, but to bring in government where it falls short. “The current insurance system is a failure,” she said. “Voters know that.” “Insurance was invented centuries ago as a form of mutual aid,” she said, pointing to ancient Roman practices where soldiers used communal funds to cover funeral expenses. “It was always meant to be a way to distribute risk collectively, so that no one would be left out.” Democrats may be moving away from tackling climate issues head-on, but in California, “climate is unavoidable,” Kim said. “It’s a crisis that’s reshaping the way so many people are living,” she said. “Losing your home, your community, your neighborhood, your schools, and then not knowing if you’re going to get insured for the very thing that you paid for? That’s unconscionable.” AI datacenters In Michigan, William Lawrence, a progressive Democrat running for Congress, has placed his opposition to unchecked datacenter expansion at the center of his campaign. He is calling for a statewide moratorium on new datacenters and backing a federal moratorium, arguing that the facilities can strain local infrastructure and drive up energy demand. Lawrence co-founded the youth-led environmental justice group the Sunrise Movement, which mainstreamed calls for the Green New Deal in 2018. He won his primary race earlier this year and will face Republican incumbent Tom Barrett in November. In his race for the state’s hotly contested purple seventh district, Lawrence has featured the datacenter issue prominently, including in multiple television ads and speeches. At least 11 datacenters are planned throughout Michigan, and three hyperscaler-size ones are proposed in district 7 alone, with another recently struck down by Lansing’s city council. The climate ramifications of datacenter buildout are important to the longtime climate organizer. The facilities consume enormous amounts of electricity, much of which is still generated by burning fossil fuels, and their rapid expansion is driving efforts to keep gas, oil, and even coal online, potentially locking in emissions for decades. Recent research found AI could increase fossil fuel production enough to generate at least three times the emissions associated with today’s datacenters. But climate concerns are far from the only reason Michigan voters are worried about the buildout of the facilities, Lawrence said. Some fear water contamination, noise pollution, higher energy bills or falling home values. Others are most concerned about the impact AI will have on the job market and society at large. “You think you know the place you live and you can envision a future there, but then you have to imagine a behemoth datacenter that … potentially driving you and your neighbors out of town,” he said. “That is all so deeply destabilizing.” The “most uniting frame”, he said, is a sense that AI companies have too much power to push projects through small communities. “That all really calls our democracy into question,” he said. Barrett does not support a national datacenter moratorium. This month he put out an ad calling for local control of datacenter development, and put forth legislation he says would stop federal agencies from overriding local land-use, zoning, siting, or permitting rules for the facilities. He had previously backed legislation which included billions in tax breaks for AI developers, and another bill aiming to limit federal environmental reviews for datacenters and other projects, the American Prospect recently reported. In Michigan, some unions and local officials have backed datacenter proposals that promise to bring jobs and revenue. Lawrence says he understands their concerns but fears AI will undermine employment in the longer term. Temporary bans, he said, would allow officials to develop stringent regulations around datacenters before their rapid buildout. A Data For Progress poll indicates that more than 40% of residents were “much more likely” to vote for a candidate who opposed the buildout of datacenters – a dynamic that helped Lawrence win 49% of the vote in Mason, site of a planned facility. Lawrence said climate-hushing is an understandable trend. “There are so many acute crises in our world,” he said. “It is challenging to name them all in a five-minute stump speech and weave it all together into one story.” Still, when he talks about the climate crisis and environmental issues more broadly with voters, particularly when discussing his own background, he said many of them are receptive. They understand that “we live on a living planet and we depend on it,” he said. Right to repair In Nebraska, Dan Osborn, the Independent former labor leader running for Senate, has made “right to repair” a part of his platform, even featuring the issue in a video ad. The policy would make it easier for people to repair and maintain their cars, farm equipment and other products, reducing waste and extending the life of goods. It’s a concept built on a simple idea: if you buy something, you should be able to fix it yourself or hire someone to do so. The candidate became passionate about the proposal after an experience at work. Osborn spent two decades as a mechanic at Kellogg’s, where he helped lead a successful 77-day strike in 2021. One day on the job, he was working with a ball valve used to flavor Fruit Loops. (“All those Fruit Loops are all the same flavors, even though they’re different colors,” he said.) He asked a co-worker in the storeroom how much replacing the valve would cost, and found the answer was between $500 and $600. Only a Teflon seal inside the valve needed replacing – a fix he said he could have made himself for about $80. But the company didn’t stock the necessary rebuild kits, meaning the entire valve would have to be thrown away and replaced. “I said, ‘that’s the dumbest thing I’ve ever heard,’” he said. “I had no choice at that point but to throw that thing in the garbage.” Osborn sees the same problem playing out with farm machinery, cars and other products, where manufacturers’ restrictions can leave workers and consumers waiting for authorized technicians or paying for expensive repairs they could otherwise handle themselves. Defense contractors run “the same monopoly repair scam”, Osborn says, forcing the military to pay contractors taxpayer money for repairs. Though he frames it mainly as an economic justice issue, he also sees an environmental benefit: repair generally uses fewer resources than making and transporting replacements and keeps usable equipment out of the waste stream. “It’s a waste for the environment,” he said. “It’s just a waste all around.” The issue has gained prominence in recent months. In July, the manufacturing company John Deere reached a major settlement with the Federal Trade Commission and five states, requiring the company to give farmers and independent repair shops access to diagnostic software and tools needed to fix up equipment. Federal and state lawmakers across the US have also proposed dozens of right to repair bills across the country. Trump has also backed some right-to-repair measures, signing a June memo directing regulators to clarify what car repairs Americans can legally perform and consider easing enforcement against people who fix their own cars. “Talking about the issue is good,” said Osborn. “But there needs to be actual laws around this, and they need to have some teeth.” Opponents, including the Cato Institute, have argued that right-to-repair laws could expose companies’ intellectual property or that improper repairs could increase emissions. But proponents say the proposals could massively benefit the environment. Planet-warming pollution from electronic waste rose by 53% from 2014 to 2020; green groups say right to repair could help reverse those projections. “I usually really talk about it as a consumer protection issue … but certainly the environment plays into it for people that are concerned about that; it gets brought up,” he said. As a candidate in an agricultural region, Osborn said many voters intrinsically understand the importance of a healthy climate and an uncontaminated landscape. “We only get one planet, and we can’t screw it up,” he said.

webTitle: Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears

fields.headline: Democrats to train tens of thousands to monitor polls amid election interference fears
fields.trailText: Project will prepare volunteers across US to monitor polls, encourage early voting and respond to disinformation
fields.bodyText: The Democrats intend to train tens of thousands of volunteers to monitor the polls and counter possible voter intimidation under a new plan to protect November’s US midterm elections from anticipated interference from Donald Trump and his allies. The nationwide initiative, dubbed the New Battlefield Project, will help state Democratic committees build up a vast coalition of volunteers to monitor the polls, push voters to cast their ballots early and create a network to respond to disinformation. The Association of State Democratic Committees (ASDC), an arm of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), plans to train volunteers across 57 states and territories. It hopes to train volunteers for 25% of the nation’s 95,000 election day polling places, focusing on districts with competitive races. These volunteers will wear blue vests to provide a visible presence intended to counter any voter intimidation, including by federal agents. Thirty state parties have a trained election protection director, with the goal of all states having one in place. The Trump administration has not explicitly ruled out sending federal agents to cities during the election, and some of the president’s allies have called on him to send immigration agents to the polls. The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, previously said immigration agents’ job isn’t to patrol polling places, but they could go to polling places if there was a threat or to serve a warrant. The president has personally made a series of interventions that have fanned fears that he could meddle in the upcoming elections, and even declare a national emergency in a bid to exert greater control over the process. Jane Kleeb, the chair of the Nebraska Democratic party and president of the ASDC, said the project is much more extensive and coordinated than the party has been in the past on election protection. “We didn’t want to be caught flat-footed on election day or leading up to election day,” she said. These volunteers will be trained to “be happy” and respond to any voter needs, including helping them find a polling location if they’re in the wrong place, or informing them they can cast provisional ballots if they need to, Kleeb said. They will also document whether others at the polls are hindering voters. “We don’t know if there are going to be a bunch of insurrectionist types out there trying to intimidate voters, but we’re going to be there happy with information, but we’re also going to be there trained to document if the other side is doing things that are violating the law,” she said. The party will additionally push out its first national early-vote campaign, telling voters to “bank their vote” by casting ballots early by mail or in person. This will include ad campaigns focused on communities at risk of Republican election interference. The state parties and the DNC typically run get-out-the-vote programs, but this year’s will include more explicit directions to voters – telling them to vote early, and not let a mail ballot sit on their kitchen counter for weeks before turning it in, Kleeb said. The party will also push for people to vote early in person. “We don’t know what Donald Trump is going to do. We’ve heard some of the things that he may do, but none of us can predict his behavior,” she said. “He’s so chaotic. All of us have witnessed certainly that. So the earlier you can vote, the better.” The third part of the project will spin up a “democracy defense network”, led by Democratic strategist Simon Rosenberg, designed to identify and counter tactics that can sway elections, including disinformation, dark money, manipulation via artificial intelligence and election subversion. The network will allow state parties to communicate with each other about these threats to share knowledge, with a goal to get ahead of such tactics before they gain traction.

webTitle: The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war | Arwa Mahdawi

fields.headline: The situation in Iran is dangerously escalating – but whatever you do, don’t call it a war
fields.trailText: Forget the bombing: the Trump administration keeps insisting this isn’t a war. But it’s not just a matter of semantics
fields.bodyText: “I will not send you to fight and die in stupid foreign wars that never end,” Donald Trump promised a crowd in Pennsylvania in 2024. While the disastrous conflict in Iran, which has escalated in recent days, may make it seem like the president has reneged on that promise, that’s inaccurate. It would be wrong to say that the president has dragged the US into yet another disastrous forever war in the Middle East because, as government officials keep insisting, what’s happening in Iran isn’t actually a war. “I wouldn’t call it a war,” JD Vance told reporters early this month, for example, after being asked whether the fighting in Iran might be over by the November midterms. “Right now, there is no active shooting.” Maybe not, but there has been quite a bit of active bombing. Earlier this month, a US missile strike hit a wedding at a private home in southern Iran, killing at least four people, including a four-year-old child and a 16-year-old. That’s fairly restrained compared to the massacre in March when a US precision-guided missile hit an elementary school in Iran, killing 150 people, including 120 children, but it’s still something I would personally file under “possible war crimes”. But not only does the Trump administration keep insisting this isn’t a real war, they’re also adamant there aren’t any real crimes being committed: the vice-president would like to stress that you shouldn’t believe your eyes or ears when it comes to the civilian deaths being reported. Despite a weapons expert and a visual analysis by the New York Times concluding that the bomb that hit the wedding party in a residential area of the country was American, Vance has a hunch the whole thing might have been made up by some untrustworthy brown people. “The Iranian state media has not been a very good scribe about what’s happened in the conflict thus far,” Vance said at that same press briefing, in relation to the wedding massacre. “So I’m extremely skeptical of this.” The vice-president may be skeptical, but I’m confused. If this isn’t a war, what is it? A little skirmish? An interminable series of special military operations? A very bloody screw-up? Trump himself has called it a war on several occasions. Last Wednesday, for example, he said: “The war is going to end immediately after the election.” However, rather confusing matters, he also recently suggested he agreed with Vance that it wasn’t a full-fledged war. “I call it a military conflict because it’s small potatoes for us,” Trump said last month. Those are some very expensive potatoes: the not-a-war already has a price tag of tens of billions. Mark Zandi, the chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, has roughly estimated that it has cost the typical US household $1,200. And then of course there’s the human cost: the thousands of lives that have been lost. What we call this “military conflict” isn’t just semantics, it matters greatly. Not least because the constitution is very clear that a president can’t unilaterally start an official war on a whim; only Congress has the power to declare a war. Trump isn’t the first president to launch major military action without going to Congress for a declaration: Harry Truman classified the Korean conflict as a “police action” to bypass Congress and presidents since have engaged in similar semantic sleights-of-hand. But, as the historian and foreign relations expert Fredrik Logevall noted in an interview with the Harvard Kennedy School: “What’s extraordinary about President Trump in the current context is that he has not really bothered to even consult with Congress, never mind seek the approval of Congress.” In other words, he’s acting like a dictator. Trump, to be fair, has been clear that he’s exploiting the Truman Playbook. “I won’t use the word ‘war’ because they say if you use the word ‘war,’ that’s maybe not a good thing to do,” Trump said at a fundraising dinner in March. “They don’t like the word ‘war’ because you’re supposed to get approval. So, I’ll use the word ‘military operation’, which is really what it is. It’s a military decimation.” Avoiding a formal declaration of war might also help the US government bypass certain “wartime” obligations to its service members and their families. Libby Klinner, the widow of an airman killed in combat operations against Iran in March, recently posted on Instagram that she wasn’t receiving certain benefits because the US wasn’t technically at war. “The Air Force recently told me that because we haven’t officially declared war, my kids and I aren’t eligible for some benefits,” Klinner wrote. “So not only was my husband killed in a war he never wanted to participate in, but now the benefits we’re left with are being dictated by semantics and public perceptions.” After this post went viral, it seems the government has stepped in smooth things over. Vance recently said the administration would ensure Klinner receives “what she is entitled to.” He added: “We will certainly work that on the back end.” The government might be able to fix Klinner’s benefits, but they’re going to have a hard time remedying the economic and political damage this not-a-war is inflicting. Trump’s popularity is plummeting, and a majority of Americans are fed up with this “small potatoes” conflict that has been going on for six months and making everyday life more dangerous and expensive. According to an estimate from Brown University last week, the conflict has cost Americans $100bn in extra energy costs. That bill is going up by $1m every two minutes. This week oil prices also climbed over $100 a barrel for the first time since July. Meanwhile, with hostilities escalating and no off-ramp in sight, it looks like Trump is out of options. All he has left is empty promises. The president has insisted that energy prices will tumble “right after the election” and, in a sign he is completely desperate, promised every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of both chambers of Congress in November. The Trump administration can call the war whatever they like, but future generations will define it as a disastrous act of hubris. Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist
